primitives.name: Measurable Cylinder Sets
primitives.verbatim_quote: Since the class of all those sets which are J-cylinders for a countable subset J of I is a σ-algebra containing all measurable rectangles, it follows that each measurable set E is a J-cylinder for a suitable J.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'J': 'countable subset of I', 'E': 'measurable set in product space', 'J-cylinder': 'set determined by projection onto J'}
primitives.assumptions: Each J-cylinder is measurable; σ-algebra generated by measurable rectangles includes all measurable sets.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure when J is uncountable or when σ-algebra does not contain E.

primitives.name: Product Measure Construction
primitives.verbatim_quote: Ifμ(E) is defined to be (Xs es μj)(E), thenμ is a measure on the class of all measurable sets andμ has the product property which justifies its being denoted by Xε 1 μi.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'μ': 'product measure', 'μ_i': 'individual measure on X_i', 'E': 'measurable set in product space'}

Each Ej is a cylinder set defined over a finite subset of indices, ensuring that intersections of such sets remain measurable. This allows for the construction of a product measure μ that respects the individual measures μ_i on each factor space. The key insight is that any measurable set E can be expressed as a cylinder set over some countable subset J ⊆ I, enabling the extension of measure theory to infinite products. The resulting product measure μ inherits properties from the component measures, particularly σ-additivity, allowing for rigorous probabilistic reasoning in high-dimensional settings.
